history.heading: First Peoples
paragraphs: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander peoples have lived in Australia for at least 50,000 to 65,000 years, forming one of the oldest continuous cultures on Earth. Hundreds of distinct nations with their own languages, laws and deep spiritual connections to land and sea developed across the continent.
Their rock art, some of it tens of thousands of years old, and sophisticated land management, including the use of fire, shaped the Australian landscape.

history.heading: European arrival and colonisation
paragraphs: Dutch navigators charted parts of the coast in the 17th century. In 1770 James Cook claimed the east coast for Britain, and in 1788 the First Fleet arrived at Sydney Cove to establish a penal colony. Over the next 80 years more than 160,000 convicts were transported to Australia.

Colonisation spread across the continent, devastating Aboriginal societies through disease, violence and dispossession of land. Gold rushes from the 1850s attracted large numbers of free settlers and brought rapid growth.

history.heading: Federation and the 20th century
paragraphs: The six British colonies federated to form the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901. Early policies included the White Australia policy restricting non-European immigration. Australian and New Zealand troops fought at Gallipoli in 1915, an event commemorated on Anzac Day.

After the Second World War, Australia welcomed large-scale immigration from Europe and, after the White Australia policy was dismantled from the 1960s and 1970s, from Asia. Aboriginal people were included in the national census following a 1967 referendum, and many children were forcibly removed from their families in what became known as the Stolen Generations.

history.heading: Modern Australia
paragraphs: The High Court's 1992 Mabo decision recognised native title, overturning the idea that Australia had belonged to no one (terra nullius) before British colonisation. In 2008 the government formally apologised to the Stolen Generations.
A 2023 referendum to create an Indigenous Voice to Parliament was rejected by voters. Australia has become one of the world's most multicultural societies.

culture.heading: A multicultural society
paragraphs: English is the national language, with a distinctive Australian accent and slang. Around 30 percent of residents were born overseas, with large communities from the United Kingdom, India, China, New Zealand and elsewhere. Christianity is the largest religion, but a large share of Australians report no religion.

Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultures, with their Dreaming stories, art and music, including the didgeridoo, are an essential part of Australia's identity. Uluru in central Australia is a sacred site.

culture.heading: Arts and lifestyle
paragraphs: The Sydney Opera House is a world-famous landmark. Australia has produced well-known writers, actors, musicians and filmmakers, and Aboriginal contemporary art is internationally celebrated.
Life is strongly oriented to the outdoors, with beaches, barbecues and surfing. Australian food reflects its immigrant communities, alongside icons such as meat pies, Vegemite and pavlova.

culture.heading: Sport
paragraphs: Sport is a national passion. Popular codes include Australian rules football, rugby league, rugby union, football and cricket, in which Australia is one of the strongest nations. The country hosted the Olympic Games in Melbourne in 1956 and Sydney in 2000, and Brisbane will host them in 2032.

politics.heading: Federal parliamentary democracy
paragraphs: Australia is a federal parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, with the British monarch as head of state represented by a governor-general. A 1999 referendum on becoming a republic was rejected.

The federal Parliament has a House of Representatives, where the party with a majority forms the government led by the prime minister, and a Senate representing the six states equally. Voting is compulsory. The main parties are the centre-left Labor Party and the centre-right Liberal–National Coalition, with the Greens and independents also important.

politics.heading: Foreign relations
paragraphs: Australia's closest security ally is the United States. It is a member of the Five Eyes intelligence alliance, the Quad with the US, India and Japan, and the AUKUS partnership with the US and UK, under which it plans to acquire nuclear-powered submarines.
China is its largest trading partner, and managing that relationship is a key foreign policy challenge. Australia is active in the Pacific, Southeast Asia and international organisations.

economy.heading: Resources and services
paragraphs: Australia has a wealthy, developed market economy. It is one of the world's largest exporters of iron ore, coal, natural gas, gold and lithium, mostly to Asian markets, especially China. Agriculture, including wheat, beef and wool, is also a major exporter.
Services make up most of the economy, including finance, education, where international students are a large export, health and tourism. The currency is the Australian dollar.

economy.heading: Challenges
paragraphs: Australia went nearly three decades without a recession until 2020. Key challenges include housing affordability, dependence on commodity exports and on China, and the transition from fossil fuels in the face of climate change, which is increasing droughts, bushfires and coral bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef.
